pos: n. (a son of Heman, head of the sixth course of the temple singers)
etymology: Hebrew Buqqiyah, wasting from the LORD, or proved of the LORD, from baqaq, to empty or pour out, with the divine name; named twice, 1 Chronicles 25:4 and 25:13.
biblical_def: Bukkiah is the first named of Heman's fourteen sons: “Of Heman: the sons of Heman; Bukkiah, Mattaniah, Uzziel, Shebuel, and Jerimoth, Hananiah, Hanani, Eliathah, Giddalti, and Romamtiezer, Joshbekashah, Mallothi, Hothir, and Mahazioth” (1 Chronicles 25:4). The office he held was instituted by royal and prophetic order together: “Moreover David and the captains of the host separated to the service of the sons of Asaph, and of Heman, and of Jeduthun, who should prophesy with harps, with psalteries, and with cymbals: and the number of the workmen according to their service was” (1 Chronicles 25:1). His father's standing and his own brothers are accounted a direct gift: “All these were the sons of Heman the king's seer in the words of God, to lift up the horn. And God gave to Heman fourteen sons and three daughters” (1 Chronicles 25:5). And the whole company was placed under one discipline: “All these were under the hands of their father for song in the house of the LORD, with cymbals, psalteries, and harps, for the service of the house of God, according to the king's order to Asaph, Jeduthun, and Heman” (1 Chronicles 25:6). Bukkiah drew the sixth of twenty-four courses, and he, his sons and his brethren were twelve.

All these were the sons of Heman the king's seer in the words of God, to lift up the horn. And God gave to Heman fourteen sons and three daughters.

All these were under the hands of their father for song in the house of the LORD, with cymbals, psalteries, and harps, for the service of the house of God, according to the king's order to Asaph, Jeduthun, and Heman.
corruption_summary: Music in worship is now governed by what moves the hearer; in 1 Chronicles 25 it is an appointed office, ordered by name and by course, under a father's hand.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern worship economy treats music as the part of the service most open to innovation, and the musician as an artist whose gift licenses him. Chronicles describes something else entirely. The singers were separated to their service by David and the captains of the host, divided into twenty-four courses by lot, numbered twelve to a course, and kept under the hands of their father. Bukkiah was not a performer; he held a charge with a number on it.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that worship is ordered by God's command and not by the taste of the worshipper, which is the regulative principle the Reformed churches confessed. The same chapter calls the singers' work prophecy — who should prophesy with harps — because they sang the words of God back to Him. A choir that understands itself that way needs no other warrant and will accept no other.

pos: n. (a son of Heman, head of the twentieth course of the temple singers)
etymology: Hebrew Eliathah, God hath come, or to whom God hath come, from El, God, and athah, to come; named twice, 1 Chronicles 25:4 and 25:27.
biblical_def: Eliathah is the eighth named of Heman's sons: “Of Heman: the sons of Heman; Bukkiah, Mattaniah, Uzziel, Shebuel, and Jerimoth, Hananiah, Hanani, Eliathah, Giddalti, and Romamtiezer, Joshbekashah, Mallothi, Hothir, and Mahazioth” (1 Chronicles 25:4). He drew the twentieth of the twenty-four courses, and his name means God hath come. What he was trained for is recorded with a number: “So the number of them, with their brethren that were instructed in the songs of the LORD, even all that were cunning, was two hundred fourscore and eight” (1 Chronicles 25:7). Two hundred and eighty-eight men, twelve to a course, every one instructed and every one cunning — the Authorized Version's word for skilled. The whole body stood under its father's hand and the king's order: “All these were under the hands of their father for song in the house of the LORD, with cymbals, psalteries, and harps, for the service of the house of God, according to the king's order to Asaph, Jeduthun, and Heman” (1 Chronicles 25:6), and the gift of the sons themselves is credited where it belonged: “And God gave to Heman fourteen sons and three daughters” (1 Chronicles 25:5).
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Eliathah, God hath come; a son of Heman the singer, head of the twentieth course of those appointed for song in the house of the LORD.
webster_full: Hebrew Eliathah, God hath come, or to whom God hath come.

So the number of them, with their brethren that were instructed in the songs of the LORD, even all that were cunning, was two hundred fourscore and eight.

All these were under the hands of their father for song in the house of the LORD, with cymbals, psalteries, and harps, for the service of the house of God, according to the king's order to Asaph, Jeduthun, and Heman.
All these were the sons of Heman the king's seer in the words of God, to lift up the horn. And God gave to Heman fourteen sons and three daughters.
corruption_summary: Skill in worship is set against sincerity, as if training were worldliness; Chronicles numbers the singers precisely because they were instructed and cunning in their work.
corruption_paragraphs: Two errors meet over this chapter. One treats musical excellence as professionalism that quenches the Spirit; the other treats it as the whole point and builds a performance. Chronicles cuts across both. The two hundred and eighty-eight were instructed in the songs of the LORD and were cunning, that is, trained and skilful, and they were also set apart to prophesy with their instruments. Skill was required because the service was holy, not because the audience was discriminating.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God is served with the best a man has and with nothing of his own invention. Eliathah's name means God hath come; the singers' charge was to say so publicly, in words God had given, with instruments the king had ordered, in a course appointed by lot. Diligence and obedience are not rivals in the house of the LORD.

pos: n. (the father of Asaph the singer; written Berechiah in the parallel)
etymology: Hebrew Berekyah, blessed of the LORD, or the LORD hath blessed, from barak, to bless, with the divine name; named once in this form, 1 Chronicles 6:39.
biblical_def: Berachiah is named once, and only as a father — but the son is Asaph. The Levitical genealogy places him exactly: “And his brother Asaph, who stood on his right hand, even Asaph the son of Berachiah, the son of Shimea” (1 Chronicles 6:39). The right hand in question is Heman's, and the office is given a few verses earlier: “And these are they whom David set over the service of song in the house of the LORD, after that the ark had rest” (1 Chronicles 6:31). The appointment itself is reported in the account of bringing up the ark: “So the Levites appointed Heman the son of Joel; and of his brethren, Asaph the son of Berechiah; and of the sons of Merari their brethren, Ethan the son of Kushaiah” (1 Chronicles 15:17) — where the Authorized Version spells the same man Berechiah. The three chief musicians of Israel are named there by their fathers, and Berachiah is one of the three fathers. Twelve psalms in the Psalter carry Asaph's name, and the man who raised him is recorded in Scripture for that reason and no other: “Praise him with the sound of the trumpet: praise him with the psaltery and harp” (Psalm 150:3).
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Berachiah, blessed of the LORD; the father of Asaph the singer, written Berechiah at 1 Chronicles 15:17.
webster_full: Hebrew Berekyah, the LORD hath blessed, or blessed of the LORD.

corruption_summary: Fatherhood is reckoned by what a man achieves in his own name; Scripture preserves this man solely because of whom he raised.
corruption_paragraphs: A culture that measures a man by his output has no way to honour Berachiah, who is on record for nothing except being Asaph's father. The Levitical registers are built on the opposite valuation. They trace the service of song backward through fathers because an office handed down through a household is more durable than a gift held by one man, and because the Chronicler wanted the post-exilic singers to know that their work had a lineage.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is generational faithfulness in the ordinary sense: raise the son, teach him the songs, and let the record say what it says. Twelve psalms in the Psalter are headed with Asaph's name, and the church has sung them for three thousand years. His father's whole contribution was to be his father. That is not a small life.

pos: n. (a priest, the father of Ezekiel the prophet)
etymology: Hebrew Buzi, my contempt, or despised, from buz, to despise; named once, Ezekiel 1:3.
biblical_def: Buzi is named once, in the verse that credentials the whole book of Ezekiel: “The word of the LORD came expressly unto Ezekiel the priest, the son of Buzi, in the land of the Chaldeans by the river Chebar; and the hand of the LORD was there upon him” (Ezekiel 1:3). Three facts are packed into it: his son was a priest by birth, the word came expressly, and it came in exile. The setting is given in the prophet's own voice: “Now it came to pass in the thirtieth year, in the fourth month, in the fifth day of the month, as I was among the captives by the river of Chebar, that the heavens were opened, and I saw visions of God” (Ezekiel 1:1). A priest's son in Babylon could never serve at the altar; the temple was six hundred miles away and would shortly be rubble. So God gave him another commission: “And he said unto me, Son of man, I send thee to the children of Israel, to a rebellious nation that hath rebelled against me” (Ezekiel 2:3), and defined the office: “Son of man, I have made thee a watchman unto the house of Israel: therefore hear the word at my mouth, and give them warning from me” (Ezekiel 3:17). The name Buzi means contempt; his son was sent to a people who would hold him in it.

corruption_summary: The call of a prophet is read as a career of self-expression; Ezekiel is sent to a rebellious nation as a watchman whose charge is to speak what he is given.
corruption_paragraphs: Prophecy is widely reimagined as speaking truth to power out of one's own conviction, with the prophet as the authentic voice of conscience. Ezekiel 1 to 3 describes the reverse. The word came expressly and from outside; the hand of the LORD was upon him; he was sent to hearers who would not listen; and his charge was to hear the word at my mouth, and give them warning from me. Nothing in it originates with the prophet, and nothing in it is his to adjust.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the watchman's accountability. A watchman who sees the sword coming and holds his peace is charged with the blood of the people; a watchman who warns and is ignored is clear. That standard governs every pulpit. The son of a man named for contempt was made to bear it, and bore it, because the word he carried was not his own.

pos: n. (the father of Mibhar, one of David's mighty men)
etymology: Hebrew Hagri, the Hagarite, or sojourner, from the same root as Hagar; named once, 1 Chronicles 11:38.
biblical_def: Haggeri is named once, in the roll of David's warriors: “Joel the brother of Nathan, Mibhar the son of Haggeri” (1 Chronicles 11:38). The margin of the Authorized Version offers the Haggerite for the name, which would make it a description rather than a patronymic — a man of the Hagarites, the desert people east of Gilead. Either way the list he belongs to is remarkable for whom it includes: “These also are the chief of the mighty men whom David had, who strengthened themselves with him in his kingdom, and with all Israel, to make him king, according to the word of the LORD concerning Israel” (1 Chronicles 11:10). The names that follow include an Ammonite, a Hittite, a Moabite and men from both sides of Jordan, and the register ends with foreign warriors standing in Israel's first rank: “Zelek the Ammonite, Naharai the Berothite, the armourbearer of Joab the son of Zeruiah” (1 Chronicles 11:39). David's guard was gathered the way David himself was gathered, from the margins: “And of the Gadites there separated themselves unto David into the hold to the wilderness men of might, and men of war fit for the battle” (1 Chronicles 12:8).

corruption_summary: Israel is imagined as a closed ethnic bloc; David's own guard list names Ammonites, Hittites and desert men who had attached themselves to the LORD's anointed.
corruption_paragraphs: Both a secular and a sentimental error run aground on this register. The secular reading casts biblical Israel as ethnically exclusive by definition; the sentimental reading answers by making the covenant indifferent to allegiance. The list does neither. It names foreigners — an Ammonite, a Hittite, a Moabite, a man called the Hagarite — as the chief of the mighty men, because they had thrown in with God's anointed king and with all Israel. Entry was by allegiance, and allegiance was costly.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the covenant was always open on God's terms and never on the newcomer's. Uriah the Hittite fought for David; Ruth the Moabitess took Israel's God as her own; Mibhar son of Haggeri stood in the first rank. None of them joined by having their former gods accommodated. They joined by attaching themselves to the LORD and to His king, which is still the only door.

pos: n. (a Danite, father of Aholiab the craftsman of the tabernacle)
etymology: Hebrew Achisamach, my brother supports, or brother of support, from ach, a brother, and samach, to sustain or uphold; named three times, Exodus 31:6, 35:34, 38:23.
biblical_def: Ahisamach is named three times, always as the father of Aholiab, and always at the point where God assigns the building of the tabernacle. The first is the LORD's own word to Moses: “And I, behold, I have given with him Aholiab, the son of Ahisamach, of the tribe of Dan: and in the hearts of all that are wise hearted I have put wisdom, that they may make all that I have commanded thee” (Exodus 31:6). The man he is given alongside is named in the previous verses: “See, I have called by name Bezaleel the son of Uri, the son of Hur, of the tribe of Judah” (Exodus 31:2), of whom the LORD says, “And I have filled him with the spirit of God, in wisdom, and in understanding, and in knowledge, and in all manner of workmanship” (Exodus 31:3). Aholiab's particular grant is recorded separately: “And he hath put in his heart that he may teach, both he, and Aholiab, the son of Ahisamach, of the tribe of Dan” (Exodus 35:34). The name means my brother supports, and the son it was given to was made the supporting craftsman to Bezaleel, and a teacher of other workmen besides.

And he hath put in his heart that he may teach, both he, and Aholiab, the son of Ahisamach, of the tribe of Dan.
corruption_summary: Creative skill is treated as self-expression belonging to the maker; in Exodus it is a gift of the Spirit, given for a pattern already specified by God.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern doctrine of the artist is that his vision is the source of the work and its justification. Exodus 31 is the standing rebuke. Bezaleel and Aholiab were filled with the Spirit of God in wisdom, understanding, knowledge and all manner of workmanship — the highest commendation of craft in Scripture — and the content of their work was fixed in advance: that they may make all that I have commanded thee. Inspiration here supplies the ability, never the design.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the dignity of skilled hands under authority, and the teaching that goes with it. Aholiab was gifted that he may teach, which means the tabernacle was built by a workshop and not by two geniuses. A man named my brother supports fathered the second man in that shop, and Scripture names him three times for it. God notices the ones who hold the other end of the work.

pos: n. (a son of Zophah, of the tribe of Asher)
etymology: Hebrew Hod, majesty, splendour, or honour; the same word used of the glory of God and of the comeliness given to a king; named once, 1 Chronicles 7:37.
biblical_def: Hod bears one of the shortest names in Scripture and one of the weightiest words: hod is majesty, the term used of the splendour of God and of the honour laid upon a king. The man is named once: “Bezer, and Hod, and Shamma, and Shilshah, and Ithran, and Beera” (1 Chronicles 7:37). He stands in the register of Asher, the tribe of the far north whose list opens “The sons of Asher; Imnah, and Isuah, and Ishuai, and Beriah, and Serah their sister” (1 Chronicles 7:30), and closes with a summary that explains why the Chronicler bothered: “All these were the children of Asher, heads of their father's house, choice and mighty men of valour, chief of the princes. And the number throughout the genealogy of them that were apt to the war and to battle was twenty and six thousand men” (1 Chronicles 7:40). Asher is one of the tribes Scripture says least about; it produced no judge, no king and no prophet, and it is remembered chiefly for Anna the prophetess in the temple at the coming of Christ. Yet its registers call its men choice and mighty, and one of them was named Majesty.

corruption_summary: Majesty has been democratised into self-esteem; the Hebrew word names a splendour that belongs first to God and is only ever lent to a man.
corruption_paragraphs: Therapeutic vocabulary has taken the language of dignity and relocated its source inside the person, so that honour becomes something a man generates and defends rather than something conferred on him. The Hebrew hod does not work that way. It is the splendour of God in the first instance, and where Scripture applies it to a man it is laid upon him from outside — a king is clothed with it, and can be stripped of it. A man named Majesty was named after something he did not own.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the quiet honour of tribes the narrative passes over. Asher gave Israel no judge and no king, and the register still calls its heads choice and mighty men of valour, chief of the princes. At the end of the Old Testament's long silence it was an old woman of Asher who recognised the Christ in the temple. God distributes majesty where He pleases and keeps the roll Himself.

pos: n. (a son of Zophah, of the tribe of Asher)
etymology: Hebrew Beri, my well, or of a well, from beer, a well or pit; named once, 1 Chronicles 7:36.
biblical_def: Beri is named once, among the sons of Zophah in the register of Asher: “The sons of Zophah; Suah, and Harnepher, and Shual, and Beri, and Imrah” (1 Chronicles 7:36). His name means my well, from the common Hebrew word for a dug well — the thing a household in that country could not live without and fought over when it had to. The tribe he belongs to is introduced “The sons of Asher; Imnah, and Isuah, and Ishuai, and Beriah, and Serah their sister” (1 Chronicles 7:30), and the whole list is summed up: “All these were the children of Asher, heads of their father's house, choice and mighty men of valour, chief of the princes. And the number throughout the genealogy of them that were apt to the war and to battle was twenty and six thousand men” (1 Chronicles 7:40). Asher's portion lay on the coastal plain and the slopes of Carmel, and Moses had blessed it in terms of plenty. Beri is to be distinguished from Beeri, who was the father of the prophet Hosea, and from Beeri the Hittite, Esau's father-in-law.

corruption_summary: Near-identical names are collapsed into one man by careless reading; Scripture distinguishes Beri of Asher from Beeri of Hosea's house by tribe and generation.
corruption_paragraphs: Beri and Beeri differ by one letter in English and are easily merged, and a reference work that merges them invents a person. Scripture keeps them apart by the information it supplies: this Beri is a son of Zophah in the Asherite register; Beeri is named as the father of the prophet Hosea; a third Beeri is the Hittite whose daughter Esau married. Three men, three settings, no overlap. Precision in such matters is not pedantry but honesty about what the text actually says.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the worth of a well. A man called my well in a dry country was named for the family's most guarded possession, the thing dug once and defended for generations. Isaac's servants fought over wells; Jacob met Rachel at one; our Lord sat on Jacob's and offered living water. A name like this one is a small window onto how Scripture's people lived.

pos: n. (a son of Shimhi, a Benjamite head of a father's house at Jerusalem)
etymology: Hebrew Berayah, the LORD hath created, or whom the LORD created, from bara, to create, with the divine name; named once, 1 Chronicles 8:21.
biblical_def: Beraiah is named once, in the Benjamite register: “And Adaiah, and Beraiah, and Shimrath, the sons of Shimhi” (1 Chronicles 8:21). The name is built on bara, the verb of Genesis 1:1 — the word Scripture reserves for what only God does — so it means the LORD hath created. The chapter opens with the tribe's founder: “Now Benjamin begat Bela his firstborn, Ashbel the second, and Aharah the third” (1 Chronicles 8:1), and tells the reader near its end exactly what the list is for: “These were heads of the fathers, by their generations, chief men. These dwelt in Jerusalem” (1 Chronicles 8:28). Beraiah is therefore a head of a household in the capital, one of the men whose houses the Chronicler set down so that a returned people could know whose they were. His name is a confession in two words, and it is the whole of what Scripture reports him saying: that the LORD makes what exists, including the man who bears the name.

corruption_summary: Creation is reduced to a process in which God is one factor among many; the verb in this man's name is one Scripture never applies to any agent but God.
corruption_paragraphs: Every accommodation of Genesis to a self-sufficient natural history runs up against the Hebrew verb bara. Scripture uses it of God and of no one else, and uses it for the bringing into being of what was not — the heavens and the earth, the living creatures, the man. A Benjamite father named his son the LORD hath created, which is a doctrinal statement made in the most ordinary way a man can make one.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the doctrine of creation belonged to ordinary households and not only to the theologians. These men were heads of the fathers, by their generations, chief men in Jerusalem, and they carried their confession in the names they gave their children. A people whose names mean what Beraiah's means will not easily be talked out of their first article.

pos: n. (a Gadite, father of Abihail, east of Jordan)
etymology: Hebrew Churi, linen weaver, or my whiteness, from chur, white linen; named once, 1 Chronicles 5:14.
biblical_def: Huri is named once, in the middle of a seven-name descent: “These are the children of Abihail the son of Huri, the son of Jaroah, the son of Gilead, the son of Michael, the son of Jeshishai, the son of Jahdo, the son of Buz” (1 Chronicles 5:14). The register around him belongs to Gad, east of Jordan, and the verse before names his kinsmen: “And their brethren of the house of their fathers were, Michael, and Meshullam, and Sheba, and Jorai, and Jachan, and Zia, and Heber, seven” (1 Chronicles 5:13). His name comes from chur, the white linen of the priestly and royal courts, so it means something like linen weaver. What the chapter is really about is given in its closing verses, where the trans-Jordan tribes win a war and then lose everything: “For there fell down many slain, because the war was of God. And they dwelt in their steads until the captivity” (1 Chronicles 5:22). Huri's house held its ground by the hand of God and kept it until the Assyrian came. The same chapter that records the victory records the term.

The sons of Reuben, and the Gadites, and half the tribe of Manasseh, of valiant men, men able to bear buckler and sword, and to shoot with bow, and skilful in war, were four and forty thousand seven hundred and threescore, that went out to the war.
corruption_summary: Victory is read as proof of divine favour permanently held; the same chapter says the war was of God and that the tribes dwelt there only until the captivity.
corruption_paragraphs: A triumphalist reading of the Old Testament takes military success as the standing sign of God's approval, and a cynical reading takes the claim the war was of God as self-serving propaganda. Chronicles grants neither. It says plainly that the slaughter went Israel's way because God willed it, and in the same breath that the tribes held the land only until the captivity. Favour was real, and it was not a freehold.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God gives ground and God takes it, and the covenant people are tenants throughout. Huri's house wove linen and bore sons and held a frontier for generations, and then the Assyrian came because the tribes east of Jordan went after the gods of the people they had driven out. The warning in that chapter is addressed to anyone who mistakes a season of blessing for a title.
